## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kesavajātaka* (Ja 346) is a canonical Jātaka story opening with the verse *Manussindaṁ jahitvānā* (“Thou that of late”) [Fausböll 1883]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha related the discourse while staying at Jetavana regarding the “Feast of Friendship” (*vissāsabhojana*) [Fausböll 1883]. The occasion arose when monks left the palace of King Pasenadi of Kosala because meals were served carelessly and without personal regard; the Buddha explained to the king that food given with affection and trust is supreme [Quang Minh Thich 2007].

In the story of the past, an ascetic teacher named Kesava falls seriously ill while being supported in the royal palace by the King of Bāraṇāsī, and none of the royal physicians are able to heal him [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. His health is restored only after he returns to the Himālayas to receive humble fare from his beloved disciple Kappa (the Bodhisatta), demonstrating that confidence and friendly intimacy constitute the supreme taste [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the king was Ānanda, the ascetic Nārada was Sāriputta, Kesava was Baka-brahmā, and the Bodhisatta was Kappa [Fausböll 1883].
